root_cause.text: The nf_tables set-iteration API incorrectly used NFT_ITER_UPDATE for operations like set deletion/deactivation that could trigger backend set cloning in nft_set_pipapo/rbtree, so an ENOMEM during an unnecessary clone left teardown paths operating on inconsistent state and hit the nft_map_deactivate WARN.
root_cause.evidence: The fix introduces a separate NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE type, changes nft_set_flush() to use it, adds comments that deletion/netns/netlink release paths “need to work on the live set” and “do not require a clone,” and updates pipapo/rbtree so cloning happens only for UPDATE_CLONE while plain NFT_ITER_UPDATE reuses an existing clone or the live set.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add a new set-iteration mode for clone-before-update operations and document its intended use.
intent_record.what: A new enum value, NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE, was added to enum nft_iter_type, and the accompanying kernel-doc comment was updated to document it as cloning the set before iterating under mutex to update an element.
intent_record.how: This extends the set iteration type interface with a distinct mode for update operations that require cloning the set before mutex-protected iteration, enabling callers to select and distinguish this runtime behavior where supported.

intent_record.intent_summary: Document why nft_map_deactivate() uses NFT_ITER_UPDATE on the live set across prepare and release paths.
intent_record.what: A multi-line comment was added immediately above nft_map_deactivate() explaining why the function uses the NFT_ITER_UPDATE iterator, including cases where it is called during the preparation phase, when a set clone may already exist from a previous command, when a set is being removed and does not need a clone, and that netns and netlink release paths must operate on the live set.
intent_record.how: This change does not alter runtime behavior; it documents that nft_map_deactivate() intentionally operates with the update iterator on the live set across several lifecycle scenarios, clarifying the expected execution context for maintainers.

intent_record.intent_summary: Use the clone-aware iterator when flushing a set so backends can clone the set during preparation.
intent_record.what: In nft_set_flush(), a new explanatory comment was added above the iterator initialization, and the nft_set_iter.type field was changed from NFT_ITER_UPDATE to NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE while leaving the other iterator fields unchanged.
intent_record.how: At runtime, set flushing now uses the clone-aware update iterator type so backends that need to clone the set can do so during the preparation phase, avoiding use of the plain update path that may not support the required cloning behavior.

intent_record.intent_summary: Handle `NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE` in `nft_rhash_walk()` the same as `NFT_ITER_UPDATE` to ensure the cloned update iterator follows the expected update path.
intent_record.what: A new switch case label, `NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE`, was added to `nft_rhash_walk()` so that it falls through to the same handling block already used by `NFT_ITER_UPDATE`.
intent_record.how: At runtime, iterators of type `NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE` will now execute the same code path as `NFT_ITER_UPDATE`, including the existing `WARN_ON_ONCE(iter->skip != 0)` check, instead of bypassing this handling in the switch.

intent_record.intent_summary: Separate clone-creation from normal update walking in nft_pipapo_walk() so update iterations use the correct existing match state and only clone when explicitly requested.
intent_record.what: The switch case in nft_pipapo_walk() was split so that NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE now handles calling pipapo_maybe_clone(set), checks for allocation failure, and walks the cloned match, while NFT_ITER_UPDATE was changed to stop cloning and instead select an existing match from priv->clone if present or fall back to priv->match via rcu_dereference_protected() before calling nft_pipapo_do_walk().
intent_record.how: At runtime, clone creation is now performed only for NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE, while normal NFT_ITER_UPDATE reuses an already prepared clone or the current protected match state instead of attempting a new clone. This avoids unnecessary or incorrect cloning during update walks and ensures the walk operates on the appropriate data structure depending on the iterator mode.

intent_record.intent_summary: Handle NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE by checking resize availability before reusing the normal update walk path and failing early on ENOMEM.
intent_record.what: A new switch case for NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE was added before NFT_ITER_UPDATE in nft_rbtree_walk(), moving the nft_array_may_resize(set) < 0 check into the new case, setting iter->err = -ENOMEM and breaking on failure, then using an explicit fallthrough into the existing NFT_ITER_UPDATE case where lockdep_assert_held(&nft_pernet(ctx->net)->commit_mutex) and nft_rbtree_do_walk(ctx, set, iter) are executed.
intent_record.how: This makes clone-style update iteration perform a resize-capacity check before walking the rbtree, aborting early with -ENOMEM if resizing is not possible, while still reusing the normal update path afterward. Regular NFT_ITER_UPDATE behavior remains the same except it no longer performs that resize precheck.

consistency_review.core_intent: Add and correctly route clone-aware set iteration/update handling across backends, including explicit NFT_ITER_UPDATE_CLONE support and early failure when cloning/resizing resources are unavailable.

relevance_review.reason: The root cause is misuse of the set-iteration API mode: operations like deletion/deactivation used NFT_ITER_UPDATE even though they could trigger backend cloning. This group adds a distinct iteration mode specifically for clone-before-update behavior and documents when to use it, directly addressing that API misuse.

The change directly concerns nft_map_deactivate() and its use of NFT_ITER_UPDATE, which is the exact API misuse at the root of the vulnerability; even though it is documentation-only, it explains behavior tied to the vulnerable teardown/update path.

These changes directly address the root cause by introducing and correctly routing a clone-aware iteration mode for set update/deactivation paths, avoiding misuse of plain NFT_ITER_UPDATE and adding early ENOMEM handling when backend cloning/resizing is required.

candidates.rationale: This flush path used the generic update iterator for set teardown/preparation, even though some backends need a clone-before-update mode. That misclassification is the direct API misuse described in the root cause.

For NFT_ITER_UPDATE, pipapo unconditionally attempted cloning. When callers used UPDATE for deletion/deactivation, an unnecessary clone could fail with ENOMEM and leave later teardown operating on inconsistent state.

The rbtree backend treated NFT_ITER_UPDATE as requiring clone/resize readiness. When teardown paths incorrectly used UPDATE, this could fail early with ENOMEM even though no clone-aware update should have been requested.

Before the fix, the iterator API exposed only READ and UPDATE, with no distinct clone-before-update mode. This missing distinction enabled callers to misuse UPDATE for teardown operations that should not have triggered backend cloning semantics.

vuln_statements.explanation: This set-iteration invocation classified a teardown/flush path as NFT_ITER_UPDATE. That API misuse is the root cause: backends like pipapo and rbtree interpreted UPDATE as clone-capable/update preparation, so teardown could spur unnecessary cloning or resize preparation, and ENOMEM during that path left later deactivation operating on inconsistent state.

In the pipapo backend, UPDATE iteration unconditionally attempted to clone backend state. Because callers wrongly used UPDATE for deletion/deactivation, this statement could trigger an unnecessary clone and fail with ENOMEM, contributing directly to the inconsistent teardown state described in the root cause.

The rbtree backend treated UPDATE iteration as requiring clone/resize readiness. When teardown paths were incorrectly marked as UPDATE, this check could fail with ENOMEM even though no clone-aware update should have been requested, causing the erroneous failure path central to the vulnerability.

The iterator API lacked a separate mode for clone-before-update operations, leaving NFT_ITER_UPDATE overloaded. That missing distinction enabled teardown callers to use UPDATE and thereby trigger backend clone semantics unexpectedly.
